extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners designing peer-review bidding/order-display systems (conference program chairs, algorithm designers, recommender-system researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating algorithms that decide the ordering of papers shown to sequentially arriving reviewers during the bidding stage of conference peer review, trading off per-paper coverage (number of bids) and per-reviewer relevance/satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper-side gain (γ_p)
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper-side gain function γp: R_{≥0} → R_{≥0} that maps the final number of bids on a paper to a nonnegative utility; the total paper-side gain is G_p = Σ_j γp(g_j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: γp is assumed to be non-decreasing and concave to capture improved gain with more bids and diminishing returns. Examples: γp(x)=√x (smooth, increasing, diminishing returns) and γp(x)=min(1, x/r) (emphasizes having at least r bids per paper). The choice of γp encodes the program's desiderata for per-paper coverage and can emphasize thresholds (e.g., at least r bids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer-side gain (γ_r)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewer-side gain function γr: [d]×[0,1] → R_{≥0} that scores showing paper j at position π to reviewer i given similarity S_{i,j}; total reviewer-side gain is G_r = Σ_i Σ_j γr(π_i(j), S_{i,j}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: γr must be non-increasing in the position (earlier positions yield higher gain) and non-decreasing in similarity. Example: Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG) style γr(π,S) = (2^{S} - 1) / log2(π+1) (the paper uses a DCG-style running example). Choose γr to capture reviewer satisfaction from seeing relevant papers early; it penalizes showing irrelevant items up-front which can cause opt-out or disengagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall gain function and trade-off parameter (G = G_p + λ G_r)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine paper-side and reviewer-side objectives with a trade-off parameter λ ≥ 0 chosen by program chairs: G = G_p + λ G_r. The goal is to maximize expected overall gain E[G].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: λ encodes the relative importance of reviewer satisfaction vs. per-paper coverage. Program chairs select λ to reflect policy; experiments and theory analyze sensitivity to λ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bidding model (f) — position-biased click model
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the probability that reviewer i bids on paper j shown at position π as a (given) function f(π, S_{i,j}), with bids modeled as independent Bernoulli random variables with mean p_{i,j} = f(π, S_{i,j}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: f is assumed non-increasing in position (captures primacy/position bias) and non-decreasing in similarity (higher relevance → higher bid probability). Example: f(π,S)=S / log2(π+1) (position-biased, relevance-proportional). The model borrows from position-based click models; independence and Bernoulli assumptions are simplifications but standard in analysis. The algorithm and objective maximize expected gains under this model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy effect / position bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical and modeled effect that items shown earlier are more likely to be bid/clicked; reviewers are more likely to bid on top-of-list papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs must explicitly account for primacy effects because ordering strongly affects bid distribution. Failure to account for primacy can leave many papers under-bid or cause reviewer disengagement if irrelevant items are shown early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity and concavity constraints on component functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural assumptions required for the framework: γp is non-decreasing and concave; γr is non-increasing in position and non-decreasing in similarity; f is non-increasing in position and non-decreasing in similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties are used in proofs and algorithmic reductions (e.g., concavity captures diminishing returns, monotonicity ensures sensible ordering incentives). When specifying gains or bid models, ensure these monotonicity/concavity conditions hold or adapt the theory/algorithms accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic for future bids (h_i): zero and mean heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: SUPER* takes as input a heuristic h_i ∈ [0, n−i+1]^d estimating expected future bids per paper after reviewer i; two examples are the zero heuristic (h_i = 0) and the mean heuristic (h_i,j = (1/d) Σ_{positions j'} f(j', S_{i',j}) averaged over future reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristics encode expected future bids to make locally optimal choices that consider unseen future arrivals; zero heuristic ignores future, mean heuristic approximates random future orderings. Choice of heuristic affects performance when paper-side gain is non-linear; SUPER* is locally optimal with zero heuristic for immediate gain and uses heuristics to guide decisions for general steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimization objective: maximize expected overall gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms must maximize the expected overall gain E[G_p + λ G_r], where the expectation is over randomness in reviewer bids and any algorithmic randomness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the formal objective for policy design. Implementations compute or approximate the expectation using the bidding model f and any heuristic for future bids, then choose permutations to maximize expected gain (SUPER* solves a per-reviewer optimization incorporating current bids and heuristic future bids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local optimality / immediate reviewer gain maximization
rubrics_metrics.description: A desired/required property: the ordering shown to the current reviewer should maximize the expected immediate gain from that reviewer conditioned on past history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SUPER* is proven (Theorem 1 / Corollary 1) to maximize expected immediate gain for the final reviewer (and for any reviewer with zero heuristic). Local optimality is a key desideratum because decisions must be made online with incomplete future information. Algorithms lacking local optimality (e.g., common baselines) can be provably suboptimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global optimality / near-optimality under structure (linear γ_p or community model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Global optimality across the entire sequence is desirable; in particular, SUPER* is globally optimal when γp is linear and is shown to be near-optimal under a community model for similarities (structured, noisy block-diagonal matrices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If paper-side gain is linear the multi-reviewer problem decouples and SUPER* is globally optimal for any heuristic. For real-world similarity matrices exhibiting community structure (e.g., ICLR 2018), SUPER* can be proven near-optimal; choose models/parameters consistent with these assumptions when seeking global guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baselines and anti-patterns (RAND, SIM, BID / fixed ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common baseline ordering heuristics: RAND — random permutation per reviewer; SIM — order by decreasing similarity for that reviewer; BID — order by increasing number of bids received so far (ties by similarity). These heuristics are standard but can be considerably suboptimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper proves worst-case additive suboptimality lower bounds for these baselines under plausible gain/bidding choices (Theorem 2). Treat fixed ordering or similarity-only ordering as anti-patterns if the goal includes equitable per-paper coverage and reviewer satisfaction; compare new algorithms against these baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposable model for computational efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A structural model class that admits faster computation: assume f(π,S) = f_π(π) f_S(S) with f_π non-increasing and f_S non-decreasing, and γr(π,S)=f_π(π) γ^S_r(S) with γ^S_r non-decreasing; then the per-reviewer optimization reduces to sorting by weights α_{i,j}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For this decomposable class (which includes DCG-like γr and f(π,S)=S/log2(π+1)), the optimal per-reviewer ordering can be obtained by sorting α_{i,j} = f_S(S_{i,j})·Δγp + λ·γ^S_r(S_{i,j}), giving an O(d log d) per-reviewer algorithm (Algorithm 3). Use this decomposition when runtime is critical and model assumptions hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational complexity / implementability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Per-reviewer computational cost targets and algorithmic tractability considerations: general SUPER* solves a linear assignment and runs in O(d^3) per reviewer; for the decomposable model it runs in O(d log d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing production systems, account for the per-reviewer complexity and prefer the decomposable model or efficient heuristics if d is large. The general optimization is reduced to a linear program with totally unimodular constraints so LP solvers can find exact integer solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational modeling assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Process assumptions underlying the framework: there are d papers and n reviewers; reviewers arrive sequentially once each; bids are binary (existence of a bid) and independent Bernoulli conditioned on position and similarity; the similarity matrix S_{i,j} is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These simplifying assumptions (single pass per reviewer, binary bids, known similarities, independence) are used for theoretical analysis and algorithm design. The paper empirically checks robustness to violations (e.g., out-of-order arrivals, repeated visits) but practitioners should validate assumptions for their deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical performance and robustness desiderata
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical targets for algorithm performance and behavior: substantially reduce the number of papers with fewer than requisite bids while maintaining reviewer satisfaction; be robust to model mismatches and real-world complexities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical results report SUPER* reduces papers with fewer-than-requisite bids by 50–75% on ICLR 2018 data versus baselines, while maintaining individual reviewer satisfaction. When judging algorithms, measure both per-paper coverage and reviewer-side metrics, and test robustness to noisy similarities, reviewer noncompliance, and other real-world effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimization formulation and LP reduction (totally unimodular constraint set)
rubrics_metrics.description: The per-reviewer optimization over permutations can be reformulated as an integer linear program whose constraint matrix is totally unimodular, so the LP relaxation yields an integer optimal solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mathematical property underlies Algorithm 2: computing weights w_{j,k} and solving a linear assignment LP yields exact optimal permutations for the per-reviewer problem. Use LP-based solvers or the Hungarian algorithm for the assignment when exactness is required and the model does not admit the faster decomposable solution.
